SHMtrace calls somatic hypermutation and other AID-driven 
mutation with a measured false-discovery rate
Abdulmateen Aderinto1,3 and Alberto Martin1,2,*
1Department of Immunology, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON M5S 1A8, Canada
2Lead contact
3Technical contact
*Correspondence: alberto.martin@utoronto.ca
Summary
Cloned-amplicon Sanger sequencing provides accurate but low-throughput measurements of 
somatic hypermutation (SHM). We developed SHMtrace to quantify substitutions and indels against 
background measured in matched activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID)-deficient controls and 
compare mutation profiles across biological replicates. A Sanger workflow quantifies substitutions 
and reports control-derived background separately. Evaluation included planted mutations, recalled 
at measured false-discovery rates of 0.050 and 0.045, simulated lineages, and twelve loci from 
eleven laboratories across four sequencing platforms. Across five nanopore assays, SHMtrace 
reduced substitution calls in AID-null controls by 64–90% relative to the uncorrected Geneious rule. 
In four assays, AID-active and AID-null libraries showed 66–141-fold separation in unique-variant 
density under the stated zero-call convention. Nanopore reads preserved mutation linkage across the 
amplicon and yielded substitution spectra similar to Sanger sequencing of the same mice. Further 
datasets extended analysis to engineered diversification and class-switch junctions. SHMtrace 
provides a reproducible framework for control-informed analysis of AID-associated diversification.
Keywords
somatic hypermutation, activation-induced cytidine deaminase, nanopore sequencing, variant calling, 
negative controls, false-discovery rate, pseudoreplication, immunoglobulin, mutation trees, Sanger 
sequencing
Introduction
Somatic hypermutation (SHM) diversifies immunoglobulin (Ig) genes in germinal-center B cells. It is 
initiated by activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), which deaminates cytosines in Ig DNA. 
Replication over the resulting uracils, together with uracil excision and mismatch repair, generates

SHMtrace · v1.3 Codex 1 · page 3
substitutions at G:C and A:T base pairs1–3. Because each repair pathway leaves its own footprint, the 
frequency, position and spectrum of mutations are key readouts of AID activity and broader lesion 
processing4–7. Relatedly, the mouse JH4 downstream intron is widely used as a genomic reporter 
because it undergoes SHM without directly contributing to antigen binding8,9.
AID activity read out from JH4 amplicons can be measured on various sequencing platforms, each 
reporting a different kind of evidence. Cloned-amplicon Sanger sequencing reads one molecule at a 
time at high per-base confidence, though it yields only tens of sequences per animal10. Short reads 
typical of Illumina sequencers give depth but may not span the complete region11. Long reads from 
ONT and PacBio span the JH4, so mutations stay linked across the amplicon, and nanopore accuracy 
now reaches modal values above 99% with R10.4.1 flow cells12–14; nanopore sequencing has also 
been used to sequence Ig genes, where consensus sequencing can absorb errors15,16. What all 
platforms, however, share is the need to separate AID-driven mutation from their own error. A wild-
type JH4 intron carries roughly one mutation per 100 bases, whereas the residual error of a single 
filtered read, especially with nanopore, is within one or two orders of magnitude of that rate and is 
concentrated at particular positions and sequence contexts17.
Two common analysis practices make this problem worse. First, general-purpose low-frequency 
variant callers judge each base by its own quality score18, and the simple rules used in commercial 
software test candidates one at a time without correcting for the number of tests19. In the 
configurations evaluated here, neither measures the errors a particular library makes, so mismatches 
that recur at one position, from PCR, sequence context or a co-amplified paralog, can be counted as 
SHM mutations. Second, treating reads from the same animal as independent replicates overstates 
statistical certainty because multiple reads can derive from the same B-cell clone or PCR-amplified 
molecule20. Matched AID-null libraries address technical background, whereas group comparisons 
must account for biological replication by using one summary value per animal. Existing SHM 
software summarises previously identified mutations21–23 but does not use matched AID-null controls 
to distinguish candidate variants from technical background.
Here we describe SHMtrace, which integrates variant calling calibrated against matched AID-null 
controls from the same sequencing run with mutation profiling and group comparisons across 
independent biological replicates, starting from delivered reads or Sanger chromatograms. We 
validated it with planted mutations, simulated lineages, twelve loci from eleven laboratories across 
four platforms, Sanger sequencing of the same mice, and deposited clones from three published 
Sanger studies, and compared it against LoFreq18, the long-read somatic callers ClairS24 and 
DeepSomatic25, the germline callers Clair326 and DeepVariant27, and the uncorrected Geneious test19.

SHMtrace · v1.3 Codex 1 · page 4
Results
SHMtrace calibrates substitutions against AID-null controls
SHMtrace starts from delivered reads or Sanger chromatograms (Figures 1 and S1). Read libraries 
undergo length and expected-error filtering28, competitive alignment with minimap229, paralog checks 
and matched-depth sampling. Sanger traces are assigned through a sample sheet and quality-
trimmed; UMI-tagged reads can be collapsed to molecular consensuses (STAR Methods).
For each substitution, SHMtrace tests read support against control error rates stratified by 
substitution type, strand and quality, incorporating position-specific background (Figures 1A and 1C). 
A leave-one-control-out margin adjusts underestimated error (Figure S2); held-out controls then set 
an empirical target–decoy threshold targeting 5% false discoveries30. This estimate depends on 
representative controls and is not a general FDR guarantee. Data-dependent candidate selection 
motivates empirical calibration rather than assuming valid Benjamini–Hochberg p-values31. Alleles in 
≥50% of reads are excluded as likely germline or parental differences; genuine dominant-lineage 
mutations can also cross this heuristic threshold, and exclusions are reported.
The read-library test can retain a candidate supported by a single read; repeated sequencing of the 
same original molecule is not required. SHMtrace uses a separate Sanger counting route (Figure 
1C): every substitution at base quality ≥ 20 is counted, and the AID-null clones' mismatch rate gives 
the expected background count, reported separately without subtraction. The germline filter, window, 
automatic checks and animal-level comparisons are shared. The Sanger results below therefore test 
trace reading, counting, bookkeeping and group comparisons, not the control-calibrated test.
Two C-to-T candidates in Sμ WT3 had similar qualities and support on both strands (Figure 2). 
Position 165, in a WRC hotspot, lacked Q≥20 control support and was retained (p = 5 × 10−19); 
position 97 recurred in controls and was rejected (p = 1). Of 743 candidates, 88 met the threshold (p 
≤ 0.009); the remainder were unresolved against background.
Group comparisons use one value per biological replicate, with log-rate Welch, bootstrapped 
negative-binomial and permutation tests (Figure 1D). Outputs include spectra, hotspot use, S5F 
targeting23, clustering, aggregate single-read estimates, junction-defined clones, read-level trees and 
power estimates (Figure S3). Desktop and command-line interfaces share the analysis engine.
Planted mutations and simulated lineages quantify recall and false calls
We planted 60 AID-weighted substitutions into each held-out control library, preserving base qualities 
and assigning 1–20 supporting reads per site, with three repetitions per control (Figure 3). On JH4,

SHMtrace · v1.3 Codex 1 · page 5
SHMtrace recalled 81% overall and 95% among events supported by at least three reads, with 2.6 
false calls per library (observed FDR 0.050). In contrast, Geneious recalled more single-read 
mutations (60% versus 31%) but produced 4.9 false calls per library (FDR 0.083). Default LoFreq 
recalled none; disabling its short-read-oriented base-alignment quality correction yielded 34% recall, 
restricted to mutations with at least five supporting reads. Permissive settings increased recall to 56% 
with 4.4 false calls per library (Figures 3A and 3D).
ClairS24 and DeepSomatic25 received peer controls as matched normals. Neither recovered planted 
events at defaults. Across 2,160 substitutions, permissive ClairS recovered none; DeepSomatic 
recalled 19%, 18%, 5% and 3% on JH4, N114 VH, Sμ and Pim1, respectively. Recall improved at 
higher allele fractions (Figure 3C), whereas 53% of 1,197 retained SHMtrace calls occurred in <1% of 
reads (Figure 2E). Germline callers Clair3 and DeepVariant recovered none, consistent with their 
intended use (Table S1).
On N114 VH, SHMtrace recalled 90% of planted substitutions, including 58% supported by one read, 
with 2.6 false calls per library (FDR 0.045; Figure 3B). Geneious recalled 88% with 2.8 false calls 
(FDR 0.050); LoFreq without base-alignment quality recalled 34%. On external Sμ and Pim1 controls 
at 2,000 reads, SHMtrace recalled 63% and 72% at FDR 0.055 and 0.035. Geneious recalled 59% 
and 64% at FDR 0.114 and 0.050; LoFreq recalled 0–26%, with permissive FDR 0.27–0.52 (Figure 
3D).
Calling the same libraries at targets from 1% to 30% tested whether the threshold delivers the rate it 
targets. At the default 5%, the pooled false-discovery proportion was 3.5–5.5% across the four loci, 
and looser targets stayed at or below their stated rate except JH4 at 10% (13.8%) (Figure S4A). 
Targets below 5% did not deliver their stated rate on JH4, Sμ or Pim1 (2.0–6.1% at a 1% target; N114 
VH, 0.5%): false calls per library levelled off while recall fell, from 81% to 17% on JH4 (Figures S4B 
and S4C).
Varying the controls through the whole procedure on JH4 showed how many are needed (Figure S5). 
One control leaves no decoys, so the threshold falls back to Benjamini–Hochberg: it recalled 68% of 
planted lineage mutations, against 93% with two controls and 95% with three or four, with false-
discovery proportions of 2.8–3.1% for the two- to four-control designs. All-null libraries yielded no 
calls with any number of controls (40 runs). One control carrying recurrent artifacts changed false 
calls little, with or without the noisy-control rule. On Sμ, AID-null controls from a second experiment 
performed like the matched controls (66–68% versus 63% recall), and pooling all five lowered false 
calls from 2.2 to 0.8 per library.

SHMtrace · v1.3 Codex 1 · page 6
Diluting real hypermutated reads into AID-null reads tested the estimates on mutations AID made, 
with their clonality and clustering (Figure S6). On N114 VH, mutation frequency was 0.87–0.97 of the 
expected value at 25–50% donor reads, and calls were made from 1–5% donor reads. On JH4, 
detection was all-or-nothing and depended on the donor: calls began at 2% donor reads for Wt3 and 
at 50% for Wt2, and no call was made below that.
Indel validation used ten planted insertions or deletions of 1–40 bp per library, supported by 1–20 
reads, with eight draws per control and error models fitted to the other controls. Among events 
supported by at least three reads, recall was 72% on JH4 and 91% on N114 VH, with 0.33 and zero 
false calls per library. Events supported by one or two reads were excluded by the three-read 
requirement. JH4 single-base homopolymer deletions were least reliably recovered (19%); recall was 
100% for 2-bp insertions and 89% for deletions ≥10 bp (Figure S7).
We next simulated approximately 40 B-cell clones per JH4 library, with clone sizes following a power-
law distribution. Mutations were introduced at positions sampled according to S5F mutability, 
including mutations shared across an entire clone, restricted to individual branches, or unique to 
individual sequences (Figure 3E). SHMtrace recalled 83% of single-read mutations versus 57% for 
Geneious, with FDR 0.037 versus 0.012 and 13.7 versus 4.0 false calls per library. In null libraries, 
false calls averaged 0.7 versus 4.3. Junction clustering recovered clone assignments with adjusted 
Rand indices32 of 0.94–0.98. When an unmutated clone contributed 60% of reads, read-weighted 
frequency was 6.2 versus a true 6.0 per 103 bp, while the majority-rule clone-weighted measure 
recovered 94% of its corresponding true burden (14.6 versus 15.5; Figure 3F).
The dominant unmutated clone could not trigger the ≥50% allele filter. Repeating the simulation with 
a mutated dominant clone showed no loss at 40% abundance, but all mutations crossing the 
threshold at 60% or 80% were removed. Read-weighted and clone-weighted estimates fell by as 
much as 62% and 34%, respectively (STAR Methods). Excluded sites are reported for inspection.
Read-weighted frequencies were within 2% of simulated truth at 500 reads (Figure 3G). Unique-
variant density varied with depth because repeated variants increase exposure without adding 
discoveries, while rare-event detection also changes. Adding the aggregate single-read estimate 
recovered 96–100% of truth; independently planted single-read events were recovered at 95% in 
aggregate (Figure S8A). Unique-density comparisons require matched depth.
Group-test calibration was assessed in 300 simulations per condition, with between-animal 
coefficient of variation 1 (Figure 3H). Under no true difference, pooled-read tests returned p < 0.05 in 
91% of 3-versus-3 and 94% of 5-versus-5 experiments. Negative-binomial rejection rates were 5.0%

and 5.7%. With three animals per group, that test detected two-fold and four-fold changes in 12% 
and 30% of simulations, illustrating the limited power at this sample size.
Matched controls set the background in real libraries
We next compared callers on real libraries with matched AID-null controls (Table S2; Figure 4). 
These included our JH4 intron libraries from germinal-center B cells of three wild-type (Wt) and three 
Aicda−/− mice, N114 hybridoma subclones transduced with AID or empty vector, and two loci in three 
assay contexts from an independent laboratory's public nanopore dataset: the Sμ switch region in 
LPS-activated B cells and in CH12 cells, and the AID off-target gene Pim1. Every caller analysed 
exactly the same reads (Table S3).
SHMtrace retained 1–4 calls across three controls per assay versus 5–20 for Geneious (Figures 4A–
4E and 4G). Geometric-mean unique-density separation was 141-, 85-, 66- and 94-fold for JH4, N114 
VH, primary-cell Sμ and CH12 Sμ, respectively, using one-event values for zero-call controls (Figure 
4F). At 500 reads, JH4 and N114 VH reached 90% and 59% of discoveries at the largest tested depth, 
without establishing saturation (Figures S9 and S10). Background mismatches were position-
dependent and separable from abundant clone-shared calls (Figure S11).
The same N114 VH reads were analyzed by IgBLAST33 and SHazaM22, which count every mismatch 
to the germline (Figure S12). With the IMGT germline the AID libraries were 2-fold above the empty-
vector libraries, because the parental line differs from it (99.3% identity) and sequencing errors count 
as mutations. Using the parental V as germline raised this to 6-fold, and masking bases below Q20 to 
32-fold, compared with 188-fold for SHMtrace.
At Pim1, mutation calls in AID-competent libraries remained close to the AID-null background. At 
2,000 reads per library, SHMtrace yielded 1.8-fold separation between groups, with four calls across 
the controls, compared with 1.6-fold separation and eleven control calls for Geneious. Increasing 
depth to all available reads (3,238–3,447 per library) did not clearly resolve the signal: SHMtrace 
detected 3–10 variants per AID-competent library and 0–3 per AID-null library, while Geneious 
detected 5–7 and 0–4, respectively (Table S1).
The two CH12 AID off-target loci, off-target 1 and off-target 2, tested a genetic perturbation expected 
to reduce AID targeting34. Off-target 1 Wt libraries carried 69, 50, and 55 calls versus 0, 2, and 0 in 
Aicda−/− controls, with densities of 3.07 versus 0.04 per 105 bases (Welch p = 9.7 × 10−4 on log 
density; 0.024 on frequency). Off-target 2 counts were 42, 28, and 23 versus 2, 0, and 0, with 
densities of 1.68 versus 0.04 (p = 5.5 × 10−4 and 0.030). G:C substitutions accounted for 97% of 174 
off-target 1 calls and 97% of 93 off-target 2 calls. MLLT1/MLLT3 double knockout reduced counts to

SHMtrace · v1.3 Codex 1 · page 8
2, 0, and 2 at off-target 1 (0.07 per 105 bases) and 1, 0, and 0 at off-target 2 (0.02), with no detected 
difference from Aicda−/− controls (p = 0.51 and 0.43). No fold is reported because a zero-count 
convention would determine its magnitude.
Leave-one-control-out error margins of five for the shared JH4 window and ten for full-length JH4 and 
N114 VH reduced held-out candidate tests with p<0.01 to 1.0%, 0.7% and 0.5%, respectively (Figure 
4H). This calibrates the error model; the separate decoy threshold estimates the false-discovery 
proportion.
Read preparation removed 67% of delivered JH4 reads overall (Figure 4I). Competitive alignment 
required an additional paralog-base filter: without it, simulated paralog reads produced 35–54 false 
variants per library (STAR Methods).
SHMtrace-generated nanopore and Sanger profiles agree in matched mice
SHMtrace processed 182 Sanger chromatograms from the six nanopore-sequenced mice, retaining 
134 clones after alignment and sequence-quality filtering for comparison across the shared 529-bp 
window (Figures 5 and S13). SHMtrace-derived mutation profiles distinguished Wt from Aicda−/− mice 
on both platforms: Sanger showed 38-fold separation (p = 8.8 × 10−4), and nanopore showed 141-fold 
separation when zero-call controls were assigned one event (p = 0.0027; Welch tests on log 
densities, n = 3 mice per group). Pooled substitution spectra were similar across the twelve 
substitution types (descriptive Pearson r = 0.92; slope = 0.97), as were positional profiles in 25-bp 
bins (r = 0.94). Among G:C mutations, 58% of Sanger and 54% of nanopore calls occurred at 
WRC/GYW hotspots, which accounted for 20% of eligible sites in the window. Among A:T mutations, 
70% and 69%, respectively, occurred at WA/TW motifs, compared with 50% of eligible sites. No 
platform-by-substitution-type interaction was detected (p = 0.62), although this does not establish 
equivalence with three mice per group. Absolute unique-variant densities are not directly comparable 
between workflows because the Sanger analysis counts mutations in individual cloned products, 
whereas the nanopore analysis counts distinct variants among 500 reads.
Sanger reanalysis recovers published comparisons and identifies discrepancies
Reanalysis of published Maea JH4 chromatograms21,35 recovered a 4.6-fold frequency reduction 
versus 4.4-fold published (one-tailed p = 2.3 × 10−4 and 0.0143; Figure S14). Spectra correlated at r = 
0.99, but denominator-harmonized frequencies averaged 1.0-fold published values. Shared trace 
assignments and identical mutated-clone pairs were retained as filed and flagged; detailed 
discrepancies are in Table S4 and STAR Methods.

Reanalysis of 402 Mkln1-study chromatograms36 found an 8.0-fold frequency reduction versus the 
published 7.8-fold (p = 0.0038 and 0.014). G:C transversions increased from 15% to 29% versus 
16% to 27% in the published tables (p = 0.0078 and 0.0040). Spectrum correlations were r = 0.97 for 
Wt and 0.62 for knockout (Figure S15; Table S4).
An independent laboratory's SWHEL study37 provided 1,795 sequences across five arms (Figure S16). 
SHMtrace recovered 2,804 of 2,809 tabulated mutations (r = 1.0000 across 60 spectrum cells), 
matching mutations per sequence to two decimals. The four substitution-class comparisons agreed 
with the publication. Total mutation decreased in both analyses, but significance differed under 
different tests. A potentially pooled host was retained; excluding it did not change the reanalysis 
conclusions (STAR Methods). The Msh2−/− arm showed the expected A:T collapse. Deposited 
sequences evaluate counting, spectra and group statistics, without testing chromatogram reading.
Long reads retain whole-amplicon profiles and within-lineage linkage
Nanopore sequencing extended SHMtrace analysis of the JH4 intron from the shared 529-bp Sanger 
window to a 1,141-bp interval spanning positions 90–1,230 (Figure 6A). Across this longer interval, 
Wt unique-variant density was 229-fold above controls. Approximately 69% of mutations occurred 
within the first 450 bp, with a seven-fold decline between the first and last 250 bp, consistent with the 
reported decline downstream of V(D)J9. Substitution spectra across the full interval closely matched 
those within the Sanger window (Pearson r = 0.989; Figure S17).
Wt mutations preferentially occurred at positions predicted to undergo SHM by the S5F model, which 
assigns mutability according to the surrounding five-base sequence. The targeting index, defined as 
mean predicted mutability at mutated positions divided by the mean across the analysis window, 
ranged from 1.22 to 1.36, indicating 22–36% enrichment over the window average (permutation p ≤ 
0.015). Calls per position were also 4.1-fold higher in the highest-mutability quintile than in the lowest 
(Figure 6B). In contrast, Aicda−/− mismatch positions showed no enrichment (index = 1.00; p = 0.50). 
Because S5F mutability is not used in the variant-calling test, this analysis provides a separate check 
that the detected mutations follow an SHM-associated targeting pattern.
Junction sequences upstream of JH4 group reads into B-cell lineages (Figure 6C). In Wt2, one largely 
unmutated lineage accounted for 81% of junction-assigned reads. Read-weighted frequency was 2.8 
per 103 bp, compared with 16.3 when each lineage's majority-rule mutation profile was counted once. 
Wt3 and Wt4 changed less (22.5 to 24.9 and 4.9 to 5.3). The largest Wt3 lineage comprised 69 reads 
and four founder mutations, with five inferred sublineages extending to 17 mutations (Figure 6D). 
70% of mutated reads fitted one tree; 7/1,128 mutation pairs failed the four-gamete test. Without

UMIs, PCR recombination and residual errors remain possible, so these are read-level 
reconstructions rather than proven cellular lineages.
Public datasets test transfer across platforms and experimental designs
Three public Illumina studies tested different biological contexts (Figure 7). At JH4 positions 53–122, 
Wt mice showed 56-fold greater mutation frequency than AID-null mice (log-rate Welch p = 0.005; n 
= 7 and 4). Ldha deletion showed no detectable difference from Wt (Mann–Whitney p = 0.75), 
consistent with the original study38 (Figure 7A).
In Aicda−/−Ung−/−Msh2−/− CH12F3 cells, ectopic AID increased frequency 40-fold over empty vector (p 
= 0.00781; n = 4 each), with one control call in 20,000 reads39. All AID calls were C→T/G→A, 
consistent with loss of uracil excision and mismatch repair; R50E yielded none (Figure 7B). 
R174E/R178E appeared more active but gave only 17% transitions, a 56% cluster within positions 
164–172 and targeting index 0.73 versus 2.46 for AID. These features suggest a library-specific 
artifact absent from controls (Figure 7C). Establishing its source would require additional sequencing 
provenance or independent material.
HMCES-deficient Ramos clones40 had 3.8-fold more deletions and 2.5-fold more insertions (deletion 
p = 1.0 × 10−4; n=6 per group; Figure 7D). Substitution calls depended strongly on a noisy AID-null 
library. A rule developed after inspecting this dataset excluded it from decoy thresholding, retaining it 
in model fitting and reporting the exclusion. Adjusted calls were 52–99 per Wt/HMCES-deficient 
clone; treating that control as a sample instead yielded 277–413. This sensitivity limits substitution-
burden inference (STAR Methods); the rule also acted in mOrange.
On dual-UMI R10 rRNA-operon reads41, consensus reduced error 57-fold (95% CI 35–99) to 0.17%, 
with residual errors concentrated in homopolymer indels. At ≥10 reads per family, substitution error 
approached one per 10,000 bases (Figure S8D). Critically, this is a technical consensus benchmark 
rather than an SHM experiment.
In the mOrange study42, inactive-AID controls calibrated active AID across empty-vector, Ugi and 
UNG contexts (Figure 7E). SHMtrace retained 115 substitutions, all at G:C, with 75–100% at 
WRC/GYW hotspots. Active/inactive separation was 20-, 1,002- and 103-fold, respectively; Ugi zeros 
used one-event values. Ugi-to-UNG transition shares fell from 95% to 4%. The paired mean 
difference was 92 percentage points (95% CI 74–110; paired t, p = 0.0021); few calls per library limit 
precision.
Two engineered-diversification datasets extended the evaluation to mutations measured relative to 
experimental starting constructs (Figure S18). In a study using a common GFP substrate43, no-editor

libraries yielded at most one call in 20,000 reads. AID substitutions were more frequently located at 
WRC/GYW hotspots than APOBEC3A substitutions, both in Wt cells (56% versus 14%; p = 0.0040) 
and in UNG/MSH2-deficient cells (37% versus 20%; p = 9.0 × 10−4). In the repair-deficient 
background, however, their transition shares were similar (78% versus 76%; p = 0.74), showing that 
transition enrichment alone could not distinguish the two enzymes.
The second engineered dataset, a CRISPR-X antibody-evolution study, diversified an antibody VH 
and published the mutations it found in each selected cluster44. Comparing the two lists position by 
position, SHMtrace recovered 150 of the 150 published mutations and called none the authors did 
not, across all 42 cluster entries (Figure S18B). Because the comparator is an independently curated 
list rather than another run of the same software, this is the sharpest available test of variant identity 
on this route.
Two further datasets tested transfer to another laboratory's switch-region libraries and to a fourth 
platform, and showed where a deposit limits what can be asked. Sμ libraries under PI3Kδ inhibition45 
confound genotype with library layout: six of nine wild-type libraries are single-end whereas every 
Aicda−/− library is paired, and the mates do not overlap, so only the twelve paired libraries reach the 
switch repeats where AID acts (Figure S19). Analysed over those repeats, the nine Aicda−/− libraries 
returned one call between them against 81–172 per wild-type library (p = 0.0021), and the wild-type 
calls carried the AID signature: targeting index 1.52–1.67 and 31–35% C→T or G→A. The calibration 
therefore transfers to an independent laboratory, platform and perturbation. The drug comparison 
does not follow from this deposit, because only one wild-type replicate per treatment reaches the 
repeats.
PacBio Sμ–Sγ1 junctions46 tested junction structure rather than calibrated mutation calls (Figure 
S20). Mean microhomology was 1.01 nt in Wt and 1.02 nt in Shld1−/−, rising to 1.69 nt without XLF 
and 1.59 nt in double mutants. Double mutants showed more ≥4-nt microhomology and fewer blunt 
junctions; Shld1−/− showed more insertions. These patterns support recovery of a known repair 
phenotype. Counts reflect PCR recovery rather than switching efficiency; 19–47% of junctions had 
alternative equally good acceptor placements (STAR Methods).
Discussion
Measuring somatic hypermutation has long meant choosing between reading molecules accurately 
and reading enough of them. This study supports a cloning-free SHM workflow by estimating 
technical background from controls. SHMtrace connects delivered reads or chromatograms to 
mutation profiles and comparisons across biological replicates. Rather than relying on quality scores

SHMtrace · v1.3 Codex 1 · page 12
alone, it estimates the background in the AID-null libraries that SHM studies already include, at the 
level of substitution type, strand and base quality, and checks that calibration by holding out each 
control in turn. Instead of treating reads as replicates, it tests independent biological samples. Both 
replacements held: 81% of planted JH4 mutations and 90% on N114 VH were recovered at false-
discovery proportions near the default target, while a quality-based caller either missed most true 
mutations or, made permissive, called as much background as the uncorrected rule, and pooling 
reads produced false positives in more than 90% of simulated experiments without a true difference. 
Together, these results support a practical route from deeply sequenced amplicons to interpretable 
SHM measurements across biological replicates.
The gap this fills is specific, and it sits between two mature bodies of software. Repertoire toolkits 
identify and summarise mutations well: IgBLAST assigns germlines33, Change-O and SHazaM 
quantify load22, SHMTool compares datasets21, and S5F models targeting23. They begin, however, 
from mismatches already taken to be real, which is why counting every mismatch to the germline 
separated AID from empty-vector N114 libraries by 2-fold where SHMtrace separated them by 188-
fold. General-purpose variant callers do the opposite: they decide what is real, but from error models 
fitted to data of a different kind. LoFreq reads base qualities18; ClairS and DeepSomatic were 
developed for tumour–normal sequencing, with different training data and calling assumptions24,25. 
The evaluated configurations did not use AID-null calibration in the manner tested here. SHMtrace 
closes that circuit by making the AID-null control, where available, the source of the error model, and 
by carrying the measurement through to the animal-level comparison that the biology requires20. Its 
distinctive contribution is to connect control-informed mutation detection with interpretable profiles 
and comparisons across biological replicates in one reproducible workflow.
Seen this way, comparator performance is a matter of operating range rather than quality. LoFreq 
was designed for deep short-read data with calibrated qualities; its base-alignment correction 
suppressed nearly all nanopore calls here, and disabling it still limited recovery of low-support 
variants. That is not a defect on its intended data: the configurations tested here did not capture this 
assay's background as effectively as matched-control calibration. The measurements say why. 
Above Q40, control error stopped decreasing and differed across the evaluated datasets (1–9 × 10−5; 
Figure S2), so the quality score runs out of information exactly where SHM calling needs it. ClairS 
and DeepSomatic recovered clean variants at higher allele fractions but few real SHM calls, and 
chemistry and model mismatches further qualify external-data comparisons. Clair3 and DeepVariant 
found none of the planted mutations, as expected of callers built to genotype a sample against a 
reference rather than to find a variant carried by a few reads. Geneious provided greater single-read

SHMtrace · v1.3 Codex 1 · page 13
recall on JH4 and Pim1 but more false calls on each amplicon. These are choices a study can make 
deliberately: sensitive mode raises the empirical target to 0.20 and recovers 72% of single-read 
mutations on JH4 and 87% on N114 VH at observed FDR 0.18 and 0.16, while events unresolved 
individually can be estimated in aggregate. Together, these outputs make the sensitivity–background 
tradeoff explicit and help investigators choose a calling regime appropriate to their experiment.
A shared framework accommodates four platforms through distinct analyses: control-calibrated read-
library substitutions, direct Sanger counting and PacBio junction characterization. A Sanger clone is 
one molecule read once, so its mutations are read directly; the workflow therefore counts quality-
filtered substitutions directly and reports the control-derived background separately. Nanopore and 
Illumina libraries carry matched AID-null arms, so each candidate is tested against the errors those 
controls make. Nanopore spans the whole amplicon, which made the 3′ decline visible without tiling, 
identified clones from the V(D)J junction and ordered their mutations into trees; Illumina gives depth 
without that linkage. PacBio combines length with per-base accuracy, and reading the donor, the join 
and the acceptor on one molecule recovered a known end-joining phenotype from a deposit with no 
AID-null arm, using junction shape in place of calibrated calls. Figure S21 sets out what each 
measured. Agreement between platforms is itself evidence: nanopore and Sanger reads from the 
same six mice gave substitution spectra correlated at r = 0.92 and the same AID-null contrast, 
supporting the use of cloning-free long reads to recover established SHM patterns while adding 
whole-amplicon linkage.
Reanalysis of public data tested SHMtrace against independent biological and counting expectations. 
Published sequence collections support reproducible reanalysis when clones are linked to animals 
and genotypes: SHMtrace recovered the principal JH4 frequency and G:C comparisons, matched 
SWHEL counts across five arms and twelve substitution types (2,804 of 2,809 tabulated mutations; r = 
1.0000), and recovered 150 of 150 mutations an antibody-evolution study curated by hand, calling 
none its authors did not. Agreement was not complete, and the exceptions are as informative: Wt 
frequencies differed after denominator harmonisation, the published Mkln1 A:T decrease was not 
significant in the reanalysis, and the SWHEL total-mutation inference differed under a different test 
(Tables S4 and S5; Figures S14–S16). The Sanger re-analysis also surfaced bookkeeping problems, 
which SHMtrace now checks and reports rather than silently resolving. By retaining assignments, 
counting conventions and quality flags, SHMtrace makes legacy sequence collections easier to 
revisit, compare and reuse.
What this enables in practice is a short experiment-to-answer path that keeps its own evidence: read 
accounting, fixed-seed sampling and one engine behind the desktop and command-line interfaces,

Limitations of the study
SHMtrace relies on representative AID-null controls prepared and sequenced alongside the samples. 
Error profiles can vary between runs and basecalling configurations, and calibration using controls 
from a different run was not evaluated. With one nanopore run per assay, the present results do not 
establish performance across independent runs.
The reported variants remain subject to technical uncertainty. Without UMIs, early PCR errors, 
recombination and repeated sequencing of PCR-derived molecules cannot be reliably distinguished 
from genuine mutations or expanded biological lineages. Mutation trees therefore describe 
relationships among reads rather than independently established cellular lineages. The default ≥50% 
allele-frequency filter can also remove genuine mutations shared by a dominant lineage. Excluded 
sites are reported for review, and experiments with a known starting sequence can use an optional 
reference policy that retains high-frequency differences. Single-read mutations that cannot be called 
individually are estimated only in aggregate, and unique-variant densities require comparison at 
matched sequencing depth.
The empirical false-discovery estimate depends on the available controls and can exceed its nominal 
target when background differs between libraries. Noisy-control exclusion requires at least three 
controls, and its effect should be reviewed. Sample-specific artifacts absent from the controls may

interpretation. At weakly mutated targets such as Pim1, signal remained close to background.
The core validation used three animals per group for JH4 and one locus per cell system. Settings 
were developed using these libraries and applied to public datasets without dataset-specific retuning, 
although the noisy-control exclusion rule was introduced after inspection of the Ramos results. 
Evaluation on an independent sequencing run with new biological samples would provide a stronger 
test of generalizability. Indel validation comprised nanopore spike-ins and one Illumina biological 
phenotype, while UMI validation used rRNA rather than SHM data. These experiments do not 
establish performance on biological nanopore indels or UMI-tagged SHM libraries; molecule-level 
consensus remains preferable when available. Two Sanger studies originated from the authors’ 
laboratory, while the independent Sanger study provided sequences without chromatograms or AID-
null controls. Together, these datasets evaluate distinct parts of the workflow, with different limits on 
the conclusions each can support.

Read preparation
SHMtrace reads FASTQ files, which may be gzipped or, for Illumina data, paired files that are 
merged on their overlap. Reads are then processed in the following order. First, reads longer than a 
locus-specific limit (2,000 bp for JH4 and 900 bp for N114 VH) are removed, as are reads with a mean 
expected error above 0.01 per base, calculated from Phred qualities28. Second, reads are aligned 
with minimap2 (map-ont preset, or sr for Illumina) against an index containing the target and any 
competing references, and each read is assigned to the sequence it aligns to best. Unmapped reads, 
reads assigned to a competing reference, reads with a supplementary alignment (chimeras), and 
reads aligned over less than a minimum length (800 bp for JH4 and 400 bp for N114 VH) are removed. 
For JH4, the competing references were a JH4-like paralog (the consensus of Agouti-type clones, 
approximately 12% divergent) and a recurrent contaminant haplotype. Because a full-length paralog 
read can align better to the longer target, reads carrying 10 or more bases specific to a competing 
reference, at sites where fewer than 20% of the sample's reads carry them, are also removed. 
Genuine JH4 reads carry 0–7 such bases, whereas paralog reads and chimeras carry 11–62. The 
fate of every read is recorded. Usable reads were then downsampled at random with a fixed seed 
(Python random, seed 0) to the analysis depth: 500 reads for JH4 and N114 VH and 2,000 reads for 
the IRCM loci. The analysis windows were positions 101–629 (529 bp, the window shared with 
Sanger) or 90–1,230 (full length) of the JH4 reference and positions 21–635 of the N114 VH reference. 
For loci whose window is not set by a preset, it runs from position 21 to 20 bases before the 
reference's end: Sμ 21–631 (611 bp), Pim1 21–882 (862 bp), off-target 1 21–988 (968 bp) and off-
target 2 21–962 (942 bp).
Control-calibrated variant calling
Each observed single-nucleotide difference within the window is a candidate, including substitutions 
supported by one read. Control error rates are estimated by substitution type, strand and quality 
threshold, combining a pooled rate with position-specific counts. For a candidate with k supporting 
reads ranked q1 ≥ q2 ≥ …, the test evaluates, for each j ≤ k, the probability of at least j errors with 
quality ≥qj, using strand-specific depth and control rates multiplied by margin c. The reported p value 
is the smallest tail probability multiplied by k.

The margin c is chosen by leaving one control out at a time. Each control is tested against an error 
model built from the other controls, and c is the smallest value in the grid 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, and 50 at 
which no more than 1% of candidate tests pooled across held-out controls reach p < 0.01. In the

What each mutation measure counts
Three measures are reported per library, and they answer different questions; group tests then use 
one value per animal. A unique variant is a position and substituted base counted once per library, 
however many reads carry it; unique means distinct within that library and does not imply an 
independent mutational origin, since one lineage's trunk mutation is one unique variant. Unique-
variant density is D / B × 105, where D is the number of unique variants and B the base 
observations at callable positions (inside the analysis window and the end trims), counted exactly as 
the read depth summed over those positions, not the number of reference positions. Because B 
grows with depth while D saturates, this density falls as depth rises even at a constant mutation rate, 
so it is compared only between libraries analyzed at the same depth (Figure S10). Read-weighted 
mutation frequency is Σ mi / (N × L) × 103, where mi is the number of called sites read i carries at or 
above the configured minimum base quality (0 for these read-library analyses), N the reads analyzed 
and L the window length; a mutation shared by many reads is counted once in each of them, so an 
expanded clone raises it. This fixed-window frequency credits every read with the whole window; an 
observed-base frequency, which counts only the bases each read covers, is reported beside it and

Quantification and statistical analysis
Groups were compared with one value per library, each library being one animal, subclone, clone, 
culture or experiment as Table S2 states; reads were never treated as replicates. The Welch test on 
log10 rates is the primary test throughout, chosen before the analyses reported here; the negative-
binomial and permutation tests are reported alongside it as sensitivity analyses, and Figure 3H 
compares all three. The negative-binomial test models each library's mutation count k with mean n·r, 
where n is that library's bases and r its group's rate, and variance n·r + φ(n·r)2 with one dispersion φ

shrinkage across features is applied, since there is one endpoint. The statistic is the likelihood ratio 
against a common rate, and its null distribution comes from 499 parametric bootstrap samples drawn 
under that common rate with the fitted φ, because two to ten libraries per group are too few for the 
asymptotic χ2. A group with no calls keeps rate zero rather than being floored. The permutation test is 
exact when the number of allocations allows, which sets a floor on the p value it can return: with 
three libraries per group there are only 20 allocations, so the smallest two-sided p is 0.10 and the test 
cannot reach 0.05 whatever the difference. Its apparent power of zero at n = 3 in Figure 3H is 
therefore arithmetic, not a property of the data, and it is why the Welch test is primary at these group 
sizes. Each cell of Figure 3H is 300 simulated experiments, so a reported share carries a Monte 
Carlo 95% interval no wider than ±5.6 percentage points (Wilson); under the null at n = 3 the Welch 
test rejected in 3.7% (95% CI 2.1–6.4) and the negative-binomial test in 5.0% (3.1–8.1), while pooling 
reads rejected in 91.3% (87.6–94.0). The Welch test uses log10 rates, with libraries without calls 
placed at their one-event density; a fold against such libraries therefore depends on that convention 
and is not a confidence bound. The same rule, one event on the library's own exposure, is used for 
every log-scale test, fold and plotted geometric mean; the software also reports each test with half an 
event and with a third of the smallest observed rate, as labelled sensitivity analyses, never as the 
primary result. The permutation test is exact. Folds are ratios of geometric means. Spectra were 
compared by pooled Pearson correlation across the 12 substitution types with a Fisher interval, by a 
repeated-measures test of the platform-by-substitution-type interaction with mouse as the matching 
factor, and by paired Šídák-adjusted t tests. Sample sizes, statistical tests, and dispersion measures
